why.headline: A strong push helps you start attacks with the ball.

claims.text: Keepers also start attacks for their team. In a youth trial, push and jump training made chest throws longer.
When you dive, your arms reach while your middle holds. Coaches of young players train the middle to link arms and legs.
In two trials, children trained twice a week on machines. After 8 weeks, chest press strength was 11.5 to 16.8% higher.
Boys in their early teens trained twice weekly. After 6 weeks, chest throws went 5.6 to 14.4% further.

keep_up.text: Keep training it every week to keep gains coming. In one youth study, jump gains lasted 8 weeks after training stopped. Everyone improves at their own pace.

map.plain: The muscles at the back of your upper arms
The muscle along your ribs, under your arm
The muscles across your upper back

note.text: Push-up studies measured these muscles in adults; none measured them in teens.

claims.text: In studies with adults, floor push-ups worked a shoulder blade muscle hardest. The wall version is a gentler start.
Studies in young people find strength rises far more than muscle size. Early gains are mostly your nerves learning to switch muscles on.

limits.text: No study has tested wall push-ups in goalkeepers. The youth trials used machines and medicine balls.
